items.title: Conventions for this development and where dependent choice and Zorn's lemma are used
items.strategy: Record that every ring here is commutative with identity and that the zero ring is allowed unless a statement excludes it. Cite the Noetherian and Artinian definitions from chain-conditions-and-semisimple-modules rather than restating them as new definitions. State the choice accounting that the rest of the page relies on: the finite-generation definition and every finite-generation argument are ZF; the implication from the ascending chain condition to the maximal condition is the one that uses dependent choice, and it is carried by thm-equivalent-characterizations-of-noetherian-modules; the maximal element among non-finitely-generated ideals used by Cohen's criterion uses Zorn's lemma, hence full choice at this library's granularity. No count, no positional claim, no scope denial about the library.

items.title: The submodule generated by a subset consists of the finite $R$-linear combinations of that subset
items.strategy: Let $M$ be a left $R$-module and $S\subseteq M$. Show the set $L$ of sums $\sum_{i=1}^{k}r_is_i$ with $k\in\mathbb N$, $r_i\in R$, $s_i\in S$ is a submodule by the one-step criterion, contains $S$ because $s=1_Rs$ uses unitality, and is contained in every submodule containing $S$. Conclude $L=\langle S\rangle_R$. Treat $k=0$ explicitly: the empty sum is $0_M$, so $\langle\varnothing\rangle_R=0$. Record that this is the module analogue of thm-generated-ideal-description-in-a-commutative-ring and agrees with it when $M$ is the ring acting on itself, so the two descriptions are not two conventions.

items.title: Every generating set of a finitely generated module contains a finite generating subset
items.strategy: Let $M=\langle T\rangle_R$ with $T$ finite and let $S$ generate $M$. Each $t\in T$ lies in $\langle S\rangle_R$, so by the previous lemma $t$ is a finite $R$-linear combination of elements of $S$; let $S_t\subseteq S$ be the finite set of elements used. Then $S'=\bigcup_{t\in T}S_t$ is finite and $\langle S'\rangle_R\supseteq T$, hence $\langle S'\rangle_R\supseteq\langle T\rangle_R=M$. Boundary: $T=\varnothing$ gives $M=0$ and $S'=\varnothing$ works.

items.title: A commutative ring is Noetherian exactly when every ideal is finitely generated, exactly when its ideals satisfy the ascending chain condition, and exactly when every nonempty set of ideals has a maximal member
items.strategy: First identify the submodules of the regular module ${}_RR$ with the ideals of $R$: a subset is an additive subgroup closed under the scalar action $r\cdot x=rx$ exactly when it is an ideal, so the two collections coincide as sets ordered by inclusion. Then transport thm-equivalent-characterizations-of-noetherian-modules along that identification and unfold def-noetherian-ring. State the choice cost in the Statement exactly as the module theorem does: the implication from the ascending chain condition to the maximal condition uses dependent choice, the others are choice-free. Everything downstream on this page cites this theorem for the ideal-level form, so it must state all three conditions, not only finite generation.

items.title: Noetherian induction: a property that passes to an ideal whenever it holds for every strictly larger ideal holds for every ideal
items.strategy: Let $R$ be Noetherian and $P$ a property of ideals such that $P(I)$ holds whenever $P(J)$ holds for every ideal $J\supsetneq I$. Let $\Sigma$ be the set of ideals for which $P$ fails and suppose $\Sigma\neq\varnothing$. By the maximal condition $\Sigma$ has a maximal member $I$; every ideal strictly containing $I$ lies outside $\Sigma$, so $P$ holds for all of them, so the hypothesis gives $P(I)$, contradicting $I\in\Sigma$. Boundary: the hypothesis applied to $I=R$ is vacuous on the left, which is why the induction starts at the top rather than at $0$. Carry the dependent-choice flag from the maximal condition.

items.title: A subring that admits a module retraction from a Noetherian ring is Noetherian
items.strategy: Let $R\subseteq R'$ be commutative rings with $R'$ Noetherian and let $\rho:R'\to R$ be $R$-linear with $\rho|_R=\mathrm{id}_R$. For an ideal $\mathfrak a\subseteq R$, the ideal $\mathfrak aR'$ is generated by the set $\mathfrak a$, so by lem-finite-generating-subset-of-a-generating-set finitely many $a_1,\ldots,a_n\in\mathfrak a$ generate it. Every element of $\mathfrak aR'$ is a finite sum $\sum a_ir_i'$, so $\rho(\mathfrak aR')\subseteq\mathfrak a$; and $\mathfrak a\subseteq\mathfrak aR'$ with $\rho|_{\mathfrak a}=\mathrm{id}$, so $\rho(\mathfrak aR')=\mathfrak a$. Applying $\rho$ to $\sum a_ir_i'$ gives $\sum a_i\rho(r_i')\in(a_1,\ldots,a_n)R$. Hence $\mathfrak a=(a_1,\ldots,a_n)$.

items.title: Every ideal of a localisation is generated by the images of any generating set of its contraction
items.strategy: Let $S\subseteq R$ be multiplicative and $J\subseteq S^{-1}R$ an ideal with contraction $\mathfrak a=\lambda_S^{-1}(J)$. By thm-ideal-correspondence-for-localisation the contraction is $S$-saturated and $J=S^{-1}\mathfrak a$. If $\mathfrak a=(a_1,\ldots,a_n)$ then any $r/s\in S^{-1}\mathfrak a$ has $r=\sum c_ia_i$, so $r/s=\sum(c_i/s)(a_i/1)$; conversely each $a_i/1\in J$. Hence $J$ is generated by $a_1/1,\ldots,a_n/1$. State explicitly that this does not assert that extension and contraction are mutually inverse on all ideals of $R$ — only on the $S$-saturated ones, which is what the cited correspondence gives.

items.title: Every quotient and every localisation of a Noetherian ring is Noetherian
items.strategy: For the quotient: by thm-correspondence-theorem-ideals every ideal of $R/I$ is $J/I$ for an ideal $J\supseteq I$, and the images under the canonical projection of a finite generating set of $J$ generate $J/I$. For the localisation: apply lem-localised-ideal-generated-by-contracted-numerators to a finite generating set of the contraction, which exists because $R$ is Noetherian. Boundary: $I=R$ gives the zero ring, whose only ideal is $0$; $S\ni0$ gives the zero ring likewise, and the argument covers both without special pleading.

items.title: A ring with finitely many ideals of zero intersection whose quotients are Noetherian rings is Noetherian
items.strategy: Let $\mathfrak a_1,\ldots,\mathfrak a_r$ be ideals of $R$ with $\bigcap_i\mathfrak a_i=0$ and every $R/\mathfrak a_i$ a Noetherian ring. Each $R/\mathfrak a_i$ is a Noetherian $R$-module: its $R$-submodules are exactly its ideals by the correspondence theorem, and those are finitely generated over $R/\mathfrak a_i$ hence over $R$. So $\bigoplus_iR/\mathfrak a_i$ is a Noetherian $R$-module by cor-finite-direct-sums-preserve-chain-conditions. The map $r\mapsto(r+\mathfrak a_1,\ldots,r+\mathfrak a_r)$ is $R$-linear with kernel $\bigcap_i\mathfrak a_i=0$, so $R$ embeds as an $R$-submodule and is therefore a Noetherian $R$-module, that is, a Noetherian ring. Boundary: $r=0$ forces the empty intersection convention, so state $r\ge1$.

items.title: A product of two Noetherian rings is Noetherian
items.strategy: In $R\times S$ take $\mathfrak a_1=0\times S$ and $\mathfrak a_2=R\times0$; these are ideals with $\mathfrak a_1\cap\mathfrak a_2=0$, and the coordinate projections identify $(R\times S)/\mathfrak a_1\cong R$ and $(R\times S)/\mathfrak a_2\cong S$ by the first isomorphism theorem. Apply cor-noetherian-from-finitely-many-noetherian-quotients. Note in a Remark that iterating gives every finite product, and that the corresponding statement for infinite products is false, with the witness on the companion examples page.

items.title: The leading coefficients of the degree-$n$ elements of an ideal of $R[x]$ form an ideal of $R$, and these ideals ascend with $n$
items.strategy: For an ideal $\mathfrak a\subseteq R[x]$ and $n\in\mathbb N$ put $\mathfrak a_n=\{\text{leading coefficient of }f:f\in\mathfrak a,\ \deg f=n\}\cup\{0\}$. The adjoined $0$ is not cosmetic: the zero polynomial has no degree by def-polynomial-degree-leading-coefficient-and-monic, so it contributes no leading coefficient. Ideal criterion: for $c\in\mathfrak a_n$ realised by $f$ and $r\in R$, either $rc=0$, which lies in $\mathfrak a_n$, or $rf$ still has degree $n$ with leading coefficient $rc$; for $c,c'\in\mathfrak a_n$ realised by $f,g$, either $c+c'=0$ or $f+g$ has degree $n$ with leading coefficient $c+c'$. Ascent: if $f\in\mathfrak a$ has degree $n$ then $xf\in\mathfrak a$ has degree $n+1$ and the same leading coefficient, so $\mathfrak a_n\subseteq\mathfrak a_{n+1}$. The index runs over $\mathbb N$ and starts at $n=0$, where $\mathfrak a_0$ is the set of constants lying in $\mathfrak a$ together with $0$; do not copy a source that displays the chain from $n=1$.

items.title: A single cancellation step lowers the degree of a polynomial in an ideal once its leading coefficient lies in a realised stage
items.strategy: Fix $n\in\mathbb N$, generators $c_1,\ldots,c_m$ of $\mathfrak a_n$, and $g_1,\ldots,g_m\in\mathfrak a$ with $\deg g_j=n$ and leading coefficient $c_j$. Let $f\in\mathfrak a$ have degree $d\ge n$ and leading coefficient in $\mathfrak a_n$, say $\mathrm{lc}(f)=\sum_jr_jc_j$. Put $h=\sum_jr_jx^{d-n}g_j$, which lies in the ideal of $R[x]$ generated by $g_1,\ldots,g_m$. Each summand has degree at most $d$, and the coefficient of $x^d$ in $h$ is $\sum_jr_jc_j=\mathrm{lc}(f)$. Hence $f-h$ is either the zero polynomial or has degree strictly less than $d$. Boundary: $d=n$ makes $x^{d-n}=1$; and when $d=0$ the alternative 'degree less than $0$' is impossible, so $f=h$ — that is the case the induction below needs and it must be argued, not assumed away.

items.title: Over a Noetherian ring, an ideal of $R[x]$ is generated by finitely many polynomials realising generators of its stages up to the stabilisation degree
items.strategy: Let $R$ be Noetherian and $\mathfrak a\subseteq R[x]$ an ideal. The chain $\mathfrak a_0\subseteq\mathfrak a_1\subseteq\cdots$ stabilises at some $N\in\mathbb N$ by the ascending chain condition. For each $n\le N$ choose a finite generating set of $\mathfrak a_n$ and, for each generator, a polynomial in $\mathfrak a$ of degree $n$ with that leading coefficient; this is a choice from finitely many nonempty sets, so no choice axiom is invoked. Let $\mathfrak b$ be the ideal of $R[x]$ they generate; then $\mathfrak b\subseteq\mathfrak a$. If $\mathfrak b\neq\mathfrak a$, the degrees of the elements of $\mathfrak a\setminus\mathfrak b$ form a nonempty subset of $\mathbb N$ — note $0\notin\mathfrak a\setminus\mathfrak b$ since $0\in\mathfrak b$, so every such element has a degree — so it has a least element $d$; pick $f\in\mathfrak a\setminus\mathfrak b$ of degree $d$. Apply lem-hilbert-basis-degree-cancellation at stage $n=\min(d,N)$, using $\mathfrak a_d=\mathfrak a_N$ when $d>N$. The resulting $f-h$ lies in $\mathfrak a$ and is not in $\mathfrak b$, and is either $0$ or of degree less than $d$; both contradict the choice of $d$. Hence $\mathfrak a=\mathfrak b$.

items.title: Hilbert basis theorem: if $R$ is Noetherian then $R[x]$ is Noetherian
items.strategy: Combine lem-polynomial-ideal-finite-generation with the finite-generation characterisation of a Noetherian ring. The proof is not compressed to a comparison of leading terms: the three preceding lemmas carry the stage-ideal construction, the single cancellation step, and the well-founded induction on degree separately. Mark this item as a landmark.

items.title: If $R$ is Noetherian then $R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$ is Noetherian for every $n\in\mathbb N$
items.strategy: Induct on $n$ using $R[x_1,\ldots,x_{n+1}]=R[x_1,\ldots,x_n][x_{n+1}]$, which is the definition in def-multivariate-polynomial-ring-by-iteration. The base case is $n=0$, where that definition gives $R[x_1,\ldots,x_0]=R$ and the statement is the hypothesis; state it rather than starting the induction at $n=1$.

items.title: $R[x]$ is Noetherian if and only if $R$ is Noetherian
items.strategy: One direction is the Hilbert basis theorem. Conversely, evaluation at $0$ is a surjective ring homomorphism $R[x]\to R$ by the universal property of the polynomial ring, so $R\cong R[x]/\ker$ by the first isomorphism theorem, and a quotient of a Noetherian ring is Noetherian.

items.title: Subalgebra generated by a subset, algebras of finite type, and module-finite algebras
items.strategy: For a commutative ring $R$ and an $R$-algebra $A$, define the $R$-subalgebra $R[a_1,\ldots,a_n]$ generated by finitely many elements as the image of the $R$-algebra map $R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\to A$ sending $x_i\mapsto a_i$ supplied by the universal property of the polynomial ring. Call $A$ of finite type over $R$, equivalently a finitely generated $R$-algebra, when $A=R[a_1,\ldots,a_n]$ for some finite list; equivalently when $A$ is a quotient of some $R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$. Call $A$ module-finite over $R$, equivalently a finite $R$-algebra, when $A$ is finitely generated as an $R$-module. Record the boundary $n=0$: $R[\,]$ is the image of $R$ in $A$. Record that module-finite implies finite type and that the converse fails, naming the witness on the companion examples page in prose only. Mark as a landmark: the rest of the page and later commutative-algebra pages cite it constantly.

items.title: Every algebra of finite type over a Noetherian ring is a Noetherian ring
items.strategy: An $R$-algebra of finite type is a quotient of $R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$ by def-finite-type-and-module-finite-algebras and the first isomorphism theorem; that polynomial ring is Noetherian, and quotients of Noetherian rings are Noetherian. Mark as a landmark: this is the form of Hilbert's theorem that later pages actually use.

items.title: Every algebra of finite type over a principal ideal domain is a Noetherian ring
items.strategy: Two lines from results already in hand. cor-principal-ideal-domains-are-noetherian states "Every principal ideal domain is Noetherian", so the base ring is Noetherian; cor-finite-type-algebra-over-noetherian-ring-is-noetherian then applies to any algebra of finite type over it. Do not reprove either input and do not reprove the Hilbert basis theorem here. In the Given line of Facts & Assumptions record the convention that def-principal-ideal-domain admits a field, because a field is an integral domain whose only ideals $(0)$ and $(1)$ are principal, so the field case falls under this Statement rather than outside it. Keep the three sections a corollary takes; add no Remark section. This is Hochster's Corollary 5.9, "A finitely generated algebra over a PID is Noetherian"; def-finite-type-and-module-finite-algebras is where this library says "of finite type" for "finitely generated as an algebra".

items.title: Finitely presented modules and finitely presented algebras
items.strategy: A module $M$ over a commutative ring $R$ is finitely presented when there is an exact sequence $R^m\to R^n\to M\to0$ with $m,n\in\mathbb N$; equivalently, $M\cong R^n/K$ with $K$ a finitely generated submodule. An $R$-algebra is finitely presented when it is isomorphic to $R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]/\mathfrak a$ with $\mathfrak a$ a finitely generated ideal. Record that finitely presented implies finitely generated for both notions, and that $m=0$ or $n=0$ are allowed, so the zero module is finitely presented.

items.title: Over a Noetherian ring a module is Noetherian exactly when it is finitely generated, exactly when it is finitely presented
items.strategy: Noetherian implies finitely generated because $M$ is a submodule of itself. Finitely generated implies Noetherian is thm-finitely-generated-modules-over-noetherian-rings-are-noetherian. For finite presentation: from a finite generating set build a surjection $R^n\to M$; its kernel is a submodule of the Noetherian module $R^n$, hence finitely generated, so a surjection $R^m\to K$ gives the presentation $R^m\to R^n\to M\to0$. Finitely presented implies finitely generated is immediate. Mark as a landmark. State the ring as commutative and Noetherian; the free module $R^n$ is Noetherian by the published finite-direct-sum corollary applied to the regular module.

items.title: Every algebra of finite type over a Noetherian ring is finitely presented
items.strategy: Write the algebra as $R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]/\mathfrak a$; the polynomial ring is Noetherian, so $\mathfrak a$ is finitely generated, which is exactly the definition of a finitely presented algebra.

items.title: Over a commutative ring the homomorphism group $\operatorname{Hom}_R(M,N)$ is an $R$-module
items.strategy: The published definition gives $\operatorname{Hom}_R(M,N)$ only as an abelian group. For commutative $R$ define $(rf)(m)=r\cdot f(m)$ and check that $rf$ is again $R$-linear — this is exactly where commutativity is used, since $(rf)(sm)=rsf(m)=sr f(m)=s(rf)(m)$ — and that the module axioms hold pointwise. Record the agreement with the published abelian-group structure: the underlying addition is unchanged, so this extends rather than redefines it.

items.title: For a commutative ring, $\operatorname{Hom}_R(R^n,N)\cong N^n$
items.strategy: By the universal property of the free module on the $n$-element standard basis, $f\mapsto(f(e_1),\ldots,f(e_n))$ is a bijection onto $N^n$; check directly that it is additive and commutes with the scalar action of the previous lemma. Boundary: $n=0$ gives $R^0=0$ and $\operatorname{Hom}_R(0,N)=0=N^0$.

items.title: Over a Noetherian ring the homomorphism module between two finitely generated modules is finitely generated
items.strategy: Choose a surjection $\pi:R^n\to M$. Left exactness of the contravariant $\operatorname{Hom}$ makes $\pi^*:\operatorname{Hom}_R(M,N)\to\operatorname{Hom}_R(R^n,N)$ injective, and it is $R$-linear for the module structure above. So $\operatorname{Hom}_R(M,N)$ embeds in $\operatorname{Hom}_R(R^n,N)\cong N^n$, which is a finitely generated module over a Noetherian ring, hence Noetherian; a submodule of a Noetherian module is finitely generated. Do not claim the embedding is an isomorphism.

items.title: Module finiteness is transitive along a tower of algebras
items.strategy: Let $A\to B\to C$ be maps of commutative rings with $B$ generated as an $A$-module by $b_1,\ldots,b_m$ and $C$ generated as a $B$-module by $c_1,\ldots,c_n$. Every element of $C$ is $\sum_j\beta_jc_j$ with $\beta_j\in B$, and each $\beta_j$ is $\sum_i\alpha_{ij}b_i$ with $\alpha_{ij}\in A$, so the $mn$ products $b_ic_j$ generate $C$ as an $A$-module. Boundary: $m=0$ or $n=0$ forces the corresponding ring to be zero and the conclusion is the zero module.

items.title: A module-finite algebra over a Noetherian ring is a Noetherian ring, and so is every ring between the two
items.strategy: Let $A$ be Noetherian and $B$ a module-finite commutative $A$-algebra. Then $B$ is a finitely generated $A$-module, hence a Noetherian $A$-module. Every ideal of $B$ is in particular an $A$-submodule of $B$, so it is finitely generated over $A$ and therefore over $B$; thus $B$ is a Noetherian ring. Second clause: if $A\subseteq B$ then every intermediate ring $A\subseteq C\subseteq B$ is an $A$-submodule of the Noetherian $A$-module $B$, hence module-finite over $A$, and its ideals are $A$-submodules of $C$, so $C$ is a Noetherian ring too. Third clause: a finitely generated $B$-module is generated over $A$ by the products of a finite $A$-generating set of $B$ with a finite $B$-generating set of the module, so it is a finitely generated and hence Noetherian $A$-module. Mark as a landmark. The intermediate-ring clause is what makes this theorem, and not only the Artin-Tate lemma, usable downstream, so state it rather than leaving it as an unremarked consequence.

items.title: A subalgebra generated by finitely many integral elements is module-finite
items.strategy: Let $A\subseteq B$ be commutative rings and $b_1,\ldots,b_n\in B$ integral over $A$. If $A$ is the zero ring then $1_B=0$ and $B=0$, so the conclusion is trivial; otherwise thm-integrality-and-finite-module-equivalences applies. Induct: $A[b_1]$ is a finite $A$-module by that theorem; $b_2$ is integral over $A$ hence over $A[b_1]$ because the same monic polynomial works, so $A[b_1][b_2]$ is a finite $A[b_1]$-module; transitivity of module finiteness gives a finite $A$-module. Boundary $n=0$: $A[\,]$ is the image of $A$, generated by $1$.

items.title: The Artin–Tate coefficient subalgebra is a Noetherian algebra of finite type
items.strategy: Let $A\subseteq B\subseteq C$ be commutative rings with $A$ Noetherian, $C=A[x_1,\ldots,x_m]$ of finite type over $A$, and $C=\sum_jBy_j$ module-finite over $B$ with $y_1,\ldots,y_n$ and $y_1=1$ available after enlarging the list. Write $x_i=\sum_jz_{ij}y_j$ and $y_iy_j=\sum_kz_{ijk}y_k$ with all $z_{ij},z_{ijk}\in B$, and let $A'=A[\{z_{ij}\},\{z_{ijk}\}]\subseteq B$. There are finitely many coefficients, so $A'$ is of finite type over $A$ and hence Noetherian by cor-finite-type-algebra-over-noetherian-ring-is-noetherian. State that the coefficients are chosen, not canonical, and that only their finiteness is used.

items.title: In the Artin–Tate setup the intermediate ring is module-finite over the coefficient subalgebra
items.strategy: With $A'$ as above, every element of $C$ is a polynomial in the $x_i$ with coefficients in $A$; substituting $x_i=\sum_jz_{ij}y_j$ and reducing products of the $y$'s by $y_iy_j=\sum_kz_{ijk}y_k$ expresses it as an $A'$-linear combination of $y_1,\ldots,y_n$. Hence $C$ is a finite $A'$-module. Since $A'$ is Noetherian, $C$ is a Noetherian $A'$-module, and $B$ is an $A'$-submodule of $C$, so $B$ is a finite $A'$-module. The reduction is an induction on the total degree of the polynomial; state it as such rather than as a single substitution.

items.title: Artin–Tate lemma: an intermediate ring over which a finite-type algebra is module-finite is itself of finite type
items.strategy: Let $A\subseteq B\subseteq C$ with $A$ Noetherian, $C$ of finite type over $A$, and $C$ module-finite over $B$. The two preceding lemmas give $A'\subseteq B$ of finite type over $A$ with $B$ a finite $A'$-module, say $B=\sum_lA'w_l$. Then $B=A[\{z_{ij}\},\{z_{ijk}\},w_1,\ldots,w_r]$ is of finite type over $A$. Mark as a landmark.

items.title: The Artin–Tate lemma with integrality in place of module finiteness
items.strategy: If $C$ is of finite type over $A$ and integral over $B$, then $C$ is of finite type over $B$ as well, so $C=B[x_1,\ldots,x_m]$ with each $x_i$ integral over $B$; by lem-algebra-generated-by-finitely-many-integral-elements-is-module-finite, $C$ is module-finite over $B$ and thm-artin-tate-lemma applies. Note that finite type over $B$ follows from finite type over $A$ because the same generators work.

items.title: A group acting on a ring by automorphisms and its invariant subring
items.strategy: Let $G$ be a group acting on a commutative ring $C$ so that every $g\in G$ acts as a ring automorphism; when $C$ is an $A$-algebra, an action by $A$-algebra automorphisms is one in which each $g$ fixes the image of $A$ pointwise. Define $C^G=\{c\in C:g\cdot c=c\text{ for all }g\in G\}$ and verify it is a subring containing the image of $A$. Boundary: the trivial group gives $C^G=C$. Record the agreement with the published special case explicitly, in dictionary style: def-symmetric-polynomial already writes $R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]^{\operatorname{Sym}_n}$ for the fixed subset of the permutation action on a polynomial ring, and that is exactly $C^G$ for $C=R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$ and $G=\operatorname{Sym}_n$; the notation and the meaning agree, so this definition extends it and does not compete with it.

items.title: For a finite group of ring automorphisms the orbit polynomial is monic over the invariant subring, so the ring is integral over its invariants
items.strategy: Let $G$ be a finite group acting on a commutative ring $C$ by ring automorphisms and let $x\in C$. Extend the action to $C[T]$ coefficientwise, fixing $T$. Put $P(T)=\prod_{g\in G}(T-g\cdot x)$. For $h\in G$ the map $g\mapsto hg$ is a bijection of $G$, so $h$ permutes the factors and fixes $P$; hence every coefficient of $P$ lies in $C^G$. $P$ is monic of degree $|G|\ge1$ and $P(x)=0$ because the factor at the identity is $T-x$. Therefore every element of $C$ is integral over $C^G$. State the finiteness of $G$ as an explicit hypothesis: the product is over a finite index set and the argument gives nothing for an infinite group.

items.title: Noether's finiteness theorem: the invariants of a finite group acting on a finite-type algebra over a Noetherian ring form an algebra of finite type
items.strategy: Let $A$ be a Noetherian commutative ring, $C$ a commutative $A$-algebra of finite type with $A$ a subring of $C$, and $G$ a finite group acting on $C$ by $A$-algebra automorphisms. Then $A\subseteq C^G\subseteq C$, $C$ is of finite type over $A$, and $C$ is integral over $C^G$ by the orbit-polynomial lemma; cor-artin-tate-integral-form gives that $C^G$ is of finite type over $A$. Mark as a landmark; it is the payoff of the Artin–Tate block and the reason that block is on this page.

items.title: If some ideal is not finitely generated, there is one maximal among the ideals that are not
items.strategy: Order the set $\Sigma$ of non-finitely-generated ideals by inclusion; it is nonempty by hypothesis. For a nonempty chain in $\Sigma$ its union is an ideal, and if that union were generated by finitely many elements then all of them would lie in one member of the chain, forcing that member to equal the union and to be finitely generated — a contradiction. So every nonempty chain has an upper bound in $\Sigma$, and $\Sigma$ is nonempty, so Zorn's lemma gives a maximal member. Flag in the Statement that this uses Zorn's lemma and hence the axiom of choice, and note that no Noetherian hypothesis is available or needed here — Noetherianity is what the criterion below is proving.

items.title: An ideal maximal among the non-finitely-generated ideals is prime
items.strategy: Let $\mathfrak p$ be maximal in $\Sigma$; it is proper because $R=(1)$ is finitely generated. Suppose $ab\in\mathfrak p$ with $a\notin\mathfrak p$ and $b\notin\mathfrak p$. Then $\mathfrak p+(a)\supsetneq\mathfrak p$ is finitely generated, say by $x_1+w_1a,\ldots,x_n+w_na$ with $x_i\in\mathfrak p$. Let $\mathfrak q=(\mathfrak p:a)=\{r\in R:ra\in\mathfrak p\}$, an ideal containing $\mathfrak p+(b)\supsetneq\mathfrak p$, hence finitely generated. Claim $\mathfrak p=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)+a\mathfrak q$: the inclusion $\supseteq$ is clear, and for $z\in\mathfrak p\subseteq\mathfrak p+(a)$ write $z=\sum c_i(x_i+w_ia)=\sum c_ix_i+ya$ with $y=\sum c_iw_i$; then $ya=z-\sum c_ix_i\in\mathfrak p$, so $y\in\mathfrak q$. Both summands are finitely generated, so $\mathfrak p$ is — a contradiction. Hence $\mathfrak p$ is prime.

items.title: Cohen's criterion: a commutative ring in which every prime ideal is finitely generated is Noetherian
items.strategy: If some ideal were not finitely generated, the two preceding lemmas produce a prime ideal that is not finitely generated, contradicting the hypothesis. Emphasise in the proof that the maximal element comes from Zorn's lemma and not from Noetherian induction, since Noetherianity is the conclusion. Mark as a landmark.

items.title: Which constructions preserve the Noetherian condition, and which do not
items.strategy: Collect the stability results proved above — quotients, localisations, polynomial rings in finitely many variables, algebras of finite type, module-finite algebras, products of two Noetherian rings, and subrings admitting a module retraction — and record that none of this extends to an arbitrary subring or to an infinite product; name the companion examples page in plain prose as the place where both witnesses are worked. Cite only items on this page. No count of the listed constructions, no positional claim, and no statement about what the library does or does not develop.

title: Noetherian Rings and Hilbert Basis: Examples

items.title: Fields and $\mathbb Z$ are Noetherian, and so are their polynomial rings in finitely many variables
items.strategy: A field has exactly two ideals, $0=(0)$ and $K=(1)$, each principal. Every ideal of $\mathbb Z$ is an additive subgroup, hence cyclic by lem-subgroups-of-z-are-cyclic, hence principal. Apply cor-finite-variable-polynomial-ring-noetherian to get $K[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$ and $\mathbb Z[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$ Noetherian for every $n\in\mathbb N$, and say explicitly that the conclusion is finite generation of every ideal, not a classification of the ideals.

items.title: $k[x,y]/(xy)$ and $\mathbb Z[x]/(x^2-2)$ are Noetherian without classifying their ideals
items.strategy: Both are quotients of polynomial rings over Noetherian rings, so cor-finite-type-algebra-over-noetherian-ring-is-noetherian settles both at once. Point out that the first has zero divisors and the second is a domain, and that neither fact is used: the argument sees only the finite-type presentation.

items.title: The polynomial ring in countably many variables is not Noetherian
items.strategy: Build $k[x_1,x_2,\ldots]$ as the union of the chain $k\subseteq k[x_1]\subseteq k[x_1,x_2]\subseteq\cdots$ of the iterated polynomial rings of def-multivariate-polynomial-ring-by-iteration, and check that a union of a chain of subrings is a subring so the operations are unambiguous. The ideals $I_n=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)$ form a strictly ascending chain: setting $x_1,\ldots,x_n$ to $0$ is a ring homomorphism killing $I_n$ but not $x_{n+1}$. By the ascending chain characterisation the ring is not Noetherian. Note that the chain starts at $I_0=0$.

items.title: The subalgebra $k[x,xy,xy^2,\ldots]$ of $k[x,y]$ is not Noetherian
items.strategy: Let $A=k+xk[x,y]=k[x,xy,xy^2,\ldots]\subseteq k[x,y]$ and let $\mathfrak a=(x,xy,xy^2,\ldots)A$. If $f_1,\ldots,f_m\in\mathfrak a$ generated $\mathfrak a$, let $N$ be the largest power of $y$ occurring in any $f_i$; then every element of $(f_1,\ldots,f_m)$ has all its monomials of $y$-degree at most $N$ or divisible by $x^2$, so $xy^{N+1}\notin(f_1,\ldots,f_m)$. Hence $\mathfrak a$ is not finitely generated even though $k[x,y]$ is Noetherian. Record the two consequences: a subring of a Noetherian ring need not be Noetherian, and a subalgebra of an algebra of finite type need not be of finite type. Work the $y$-degree bookkeeping explicitly rather than asserting it.

items.title: The subring $k[x,x/y,x/y^2,\ldots]$ of $k(x,y)$ has a strictly ascending chain of principal ideals
items.strategy: Inside $\operatorname{Frac}(k[x,y])$, which exists because $k[x,y]$ is a domain, let $R=k[x,x/y,x/y^2,\ldots]$. Then $(x)\subseteq(x/y)\subseteq(x/y^2)\subseteq\cdots$ because $x=y\cdot(x/y)$ and generally $x/y^n=y\cdot(x/y^{n+1})$; show each inclusion is strict by a degree-in-$y$ argument on the representations available in $R$. Conclude non-Noetherian from the ascending chain condition. Contrast with the previous example: there the failure is in a finitely generated ideal's generators, here in an unbounded chain of principal ideals.

items.title: Working the Hilbert basis construction on an ideal of $\mathbb Z[x]$ with non-monic stages
items.strategy: Take $\mathfrak a=(2x,3x^2,x^3)\subseteq\mathbb Z[x]$ and compute the stage ideals $\mathfrak a_0,\mathfrak a_1,\mathfrak a_2,\mathfrak a_3,\ldots$ of lem-leading-coefficient-ideals explicitly, including $\mathfrak a_0=0$, identifying where the chain stabilises and why. Then run one cancellation step of lem-hilbert-basis-degree-cancellation on an element of degree above the stabilisation index, and exhibit the finite generating set that lem-polynomial-ideal-finite-generation produces. The point of the example is the non-monic leading coefficients, where the reduction cannot simply divide.

items.title: Identifying the coefficient algebra in a concrete Artin–Tate tower
items.strategy: Take $A=k$, $C=k[t]$, and $B=k[t^2,t^3]$, so that $C$ is of finite type over $k$ and module-finite over $B$ with module generators $1,t$. Write out the relations $t=z_{11}\cdot1+z_{12}t$ and $t\cdot t=z_{111}\cdot1+z_{112}t$ with coefficients in $B$, exhibit the finitely many coefficients that lem-artin-tate-coefficient-subalgebra collects, and check that the resulting $A'$ is of finite type over $k$ and that $B$ is a finite $A'$-module. Conclude with thm-artin-tate-lemma that $B$ is of finite type over $k$, and confirm directly that $B=k[t^2,t^3]$.

items.title: False statement: in a Noetherian ring there is a single bound on the number of generators an ideal needs
items.strategy: Refute in $k[x,y]$, which is Noetherian. The ideal $(x,y)^n$ needs at least $n+1$ generators: if $g_1,\ldots,g_m$ generate it, write each monomial $x^iy^{n-i}$ as $\sum h_jg_j$ and compare homogeneous parts of degree $n$; the degree-$n$ components of the $g_j$ then span the $(n+1)$-dimensional space of degree-$n$ forms over $k$, so $m\ge n+1$. Since $n$ is arbitrary, no uniform bound exists. State that the Noetherian condition bounds each ideal separately and asserts nothing uniform, and set up the graded decomposition of $k[x,y]$ explicitly rather than assuming it.

items.title: An algebra that is finite dimensional as a vector space over a field is a Noetherian ring
items.strategy: Let $A$ be a commutative $k$-algebra whose underlying $k$-vector space is finite dimensional. Every ideal of $A$ is in particular a $k$-subspace, hence finite dimensional by thm-dimension-of-a-linear-subspace, so a finite $k$-basis of it generates it as an ideal. Note that this gives module finiteness over $k$ and so also follows from thm-module-finite-algebra-over-a-noetherian-ring-is-noetherian; give the direct argument and record the agreement.

items.title: The symmetric polynomials as the invariant ring of the symmetric group, seen through Noether's finiteness theorem
items.strategy: Let $S_n$ act on $k[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$ by permuting the indeterminates; this is an action by $k$-algebra automorphisms, and its invariant subring is the ring of symmetric polynomials of def-symmetric-polynomial. Noether's finiteness theorem says only that this invariant ring is of finite type over $k$; thm-fundamental-theorem-of-symmetric-polynomials says more, namely that the elementary symmetric polynomials generate it. Check that the two statements agree and say precisely what the extra content of the classical theorem is. Also run the orbit polynomial of lem-orbit-polynomial-has-invariant-coefficients on $x_1$ and identify it with $\prod_{i}(T-x_i)$ raised to the appropriate power, whose coefficients are the elementary symmetric polynomials up to sign.

items.title: When the group order is invertible the Reynolds operator retracts a ring onto its invariants
items.strategy: Let a finite group $G$ of order $n$ act on a commutative ring $S$ by ring automorphisms and suppose the image of $n$ is invertible in $S$. Define $\rho(s)=\frac1n\sum_{g\in G}g(s)$ and check three things: $\rho(s)$ is invariant, because $h\rho(s)=\frac1n\sum_{g}(hg)(s)=\rho(s)$ as $g\mapsto hg$ permutes $G$; $\rho$ is $S^G$-linear, because $g(as)=g(a)g(s)=ag(s)$ for invariant $a$; and $\rho$ fixes $S^G$ pointwise. So $\rho$ is a retraction of the inclusion $S^G\subseteq S$ as a map of $S^G$-modules, and lem-retract-of-a-noetherian-ring-is-noetherian gives that $S^G$ is Noetherian whenever $S$ is. Say what this buys over thm-noether-finiteness-theorem-for-invariants: it drops the finite-type hypothesis on $S$ but adds the hypothesis that $n$ is invertible, so neither statement contains the other. Give the characteristic-$p$ caveat concretely: if the characteristic of a field in $S$ divides $n$, the operator is not defined.

items.title: $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Z}(\mathbb Z/m,\mathbb Z/n)\cong\mathbb Z/\gcd(m,n)$
items.strategy: A homomorphism is determined by the image of $1+m\mathbb Z$, which must be killed by $m$; the elements of $\mathbb Z/n$ killed by $m$ form the subgroup generated by $n/\gcd(m,n)$, of order $\gcd(m,n)$. Check that the resulting bijection is $\mathbb Z$-linear for the module structure of lem-hom-module-over-a-commutative-ring. This is a finitely generated module, as cor-hom-of-finite-modules-is-finite-over-a-noetherian-ring predicts, and here the module is computed outright. Handle $m=0$ or $n=0$ explicitly with the convention $\gcd(m,0)=|m|$.
